World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Mother's Day gratitude from a former foster child
World.content:
Unsure if he was lovable as a child, Jaharn recalls the dread he felt when Mother's Day was celebrated at school. Watching his friends greet and hug their parents while he remained alone was confusing.

One question dominated his thoughts: "Why don't my parents love me?"

That anxiety is no longer a concern for the confident 19-year-old, who grew up in out-of-home care and holds his own when advocating with some of Australia's most seasoned politicians.

There is certainty in the knowledge that his mum cares for him by choice and he lives in a home that is consistently secure and loving.

This Sunday, Jaharn Mundy-Drazevich will honour Selina Walker, the Ngunnawal woman who "became one of the strongest parental figures, not just in my life, but in the wider community".

"If she wasn't there, I honestly don't know where I would have ended up," said the Yuin, Ngunnawal and Ngarigo man.

"She didn't have to take us on, but she did."

Jaharn, as a young kid, soaking up the sun and surf on a family holiday. (Supplied)

At the tender age of two-months-old Jaharn was removed from his birth parents and then placed in a series of different foster homes. After an incident where he said he was badly burned, he found his way to his forever home.

Selina was 29 years-old when she made the decision to be a kinship foster parent.

"When I was told that they were going to have to go to foster care because I couldn't find any other kinship carers, that's when I decided that I would take [Jaharn] into my care," she says

Young Jaharn was accompanied by six closely aged relatives.

Settling in and building a family took more than a decade, according to the woman who raised Jaharn as a single parent.

Selina remembers that Jaharn's big lesson was "to let go of the parenting; that I was the adult".

"I had to demonstrate to him that I'm not going anywhere," she said.

"I'm not abandoning you. I look after the other [children] … so he could actually just be a kid."

Selina said being a foster carer was "not easy work".

"It is very tough trying to raise a traumatised child. But the reward is seeing them thrive and, like with Jaharn, wanting to give back [to the community]. This has been our cultural way for a very long time.

" It's just about supporting them to find their feet through the chaos. "

Now an adult, Jaharn (pictured here with Selina) wants to advocate for kids like him. (Supplied/ ABC graphics)

Selina has been a foster mother for more than 20 years and is currently the kinship carer of nine children.

The foster carer was recognised for her efforts in 2017 when she was named the ACT's Barnardos' Mother of the Year, and more recently when awarded the 2024 ACT Australian of the Year Local Hero.

Selina is a founding member of Yerrabi Yurwang Child and Family Aboriginal Corporation, a community-controlled organisation helping Indigenous families and children.

Winners are grinners! Jaharn said his childhood was better because of his foster mother. (Supplied)

Jaharn credits Selina as responsible for the young man he is today, through her unconditional love.

He is keen to work within the mental health sector with children and teenagers, having been inspired by Selina, he said.

"I'm on several youth advisory boards and groups now," Jaharn said.

"I want to do a bachelor's degree in social work and to work in the care and protection role or as a caseworker.

"I want to help them and be a stable guide and mentor."

Throughout his early life, there were times when dreams of university seemed beyond his imagination.

"I've gone through a lot of mental health challenges," he said.

" I always tell everyone that I'm a proud blackfella but growing up and not knowing who my family was and where we actually came from … that sense of identity wasn't always [as] clear as it is today. "

About seven years ago, he learnt of his Yuin heritage, from the south coast of NSW.

Jaharn hopes he can help children like his foster mother, Selina, has. (Supplied: SNAICC)

At a funeral for his grandfather two years ago, he finally met his aunties, uncles and cousins.

"That first real connection came through Sorry Business, which made the experience meaningful but also heavy."

Lived experience drives his advocacy to ensure all Aboriginal youth in out-of-home care and their carers are case managed by Aboriginal community-controlled agencies.

His passion to see young people maintain ties to their community saw Jaharn standing next to Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek at Parliament House, where they addressed a crowd in March this year.

Jaharn joined an alliance of organisations, including the national voice for Aboriginal children — SNAICC — to call on the government to urgently address the high rates of Indigenous children in out-of-home care.

Jaharn was invited to share at a Closing the Gap event. (Supplied: SNAICC)

Under the National Closing the Gap Agreement, all governments made a commitment to reduce the number of Indigenous youth in the system.

However, the latest data shows Indigenous children are about 10 times more likely to be in out-of-home care than other Australians.

Catherine Liddle the CEO of SNAICC also spoke at the event and said Indigenous families caring for Indigenous children is paramount.

"We know that children that are completely disconnected from their families are more likely to self-harm," she said.

"We know they're more likely to come into contact with juvenile justice systems. We know that it is a really hard road.

"There is a way to make that easier for children and that is by ensuring they have connections to who they are, and they know there are people behind them who love them for who they are."

Looking towards the future

Selina is proud of the young man Jaharn has become and is confident that he will be successful in whatever he wants to do in life.

"The proof is in the pudding and that's where you can see it in Jaharn ... [who has] become a strong, contributing Black man in society," Selina said.

Jaharn is also learning more about his culture and family connections, which he wasn't aware of while growing up in Canberra.

"Culture means a lot to me. Making those connections now, I've been able to do family history where I've been able to go back through generations … that's what I've always wanted," said Jaharn with a smile.

World.title: Some nannies working without superannuation due to 'discriminatory' law
World.content:
Despite working full-time hours as a nanny, Jess Renn has not been paid superannuation for more than two decades.

The Melbourne woman works up to 50 hours each week, typically across two families.

"I've worked [a maximum of] 30 hours [with] one family and 20 hours [with] another family, so that's where it has greatly affected me because [in] any other job, those are full-time hours," she said.

"But because I work across multiple clients, it then becomes an issue."

Under current laws, it is not compulsory for domestic workers employed in private homes, such as cleaners, housekeepers and nannies, working less than 30 hours a week, to receive super.

The 30-hour cap was originally introduced to prevent superannuation fund fees from eroding low-balance superannuation accounts.

But now, there are fee protections on small superannuation balances to ensure this does not happen.

Jess Renn has not been paid superannuation for more than two decades. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

When Ms Renn asked her employers about being paid superannuation, she said they told her they were not legally obliged.

"[With] one long-term family, I negotiated instead of a pay rise, I would salary sacrifice my pay rise into my super," she said.

"I realised I have maybe 25 per cent of super than any other person [at my age] may have in their bank right now."

Analysis from Super Members Council (SMC), the peak body for profit-to-members superannuation funds, shows nearly 40,000 domestic workers will be affected during the 2026–27 financial year, with each person missing out on about $4,000 a year, on average.

The lost superannuation adds up to nearly $150 million nationwide.

Super peak body calls for change to regulations

The council is calling for the federal government to scrap the "outdated and discriminatory" law. The change could leave domestic workers retiring with about $130,000 more in superannuation.

With women retiring with 25 per cent less superannuation than men, SMC said this change would help to reduce the gap, given 86 per cent of domestic workers were women.

Some domestic employees in private homes are missing out on superannuation. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

"Domestic workers are doing essential paid work, yet the system still treats them as second-class workers when it comes to superannuation, and that burden falls overwhelmingly on women," said CEO Misha Schubert.

"When something is outdated, you fix it. Fixing these outdated laws would help close the gender superannuation gap and boost the retirement savings of thousands of hardworking Australians."

Workers try to catch up by making voluntary contributions

Another nanny, Ellen, who has asked the ABC to only use her first name, said one family she worked for made sure she never worked more than 30 hours a week.

The Super Members Council is calling for the federal government to scrap an "outdated and discriminatory" law. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

"They would cut me bang on 29.5 [hours]. If it was looking like I was getting close, they'd go, 'Oh, go home', because they would not, they did not, want to pay me any super," she said.

Ellen said she tried to negotiate superannuation contributions with this family, but was knocked back.

"I confronted them, and they just bluntly said, 'Well, we don't legally have to because we keep your hours under 30 hours,'" she said.

" It took me years to negotiate my rate higher so that I could pay my own super. "

It has meant that she has missed out on years of employer contributions and compounding interest, which will ultimately affect her retirement.

"I am paying for that now myself by trying to bank an extra $50 a week into my superannuation so that I'm not falling behind … and I'm going to probably have to rely to some extent on my husband's superannuation and if I wasn't with him, I'd probably be in a lot of trouble."

The 30-hour cap on contributions was to prevent super fund fees eroding low-balance accounts. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

A 'power imbalance' between worker and family

Lauren Brown is the owner of payroll facilitation service Nanny Pay, which she said she created to ensure nannies were supported.

"This rule is leaving a loophole where people do not have to pay super, and … it just makes a wider pattern, and it makes it more complicated for people to do the right thing for their financial future," she said.

Lauren Brown says it is hard for nannies to financially prepare for their future. (Supplied: Lauren Brown)

Ms Brown said there was already a power imbalance between a family and a nanny, and the superannuation law exacerbated that.

"When the domestic super rule is the reason why families can say no, it makes that negotiation so much harder for that worker," she said.

"Women are already missing out on super because of maternity leave and raising children. It's just a systemic problem that this rule plays a big role in."

However, Mark Hudson, who is the managing director of another payroll facilitation service, Pay the Nanny, said he could see both sides.

Mark Hudson says nannies are being denied important employment rights. (Supplied: Mark Hudson)

"Lots of nannies might be doing two or three hours here and there, or might be a working-holiday maker," he said.

"Adding superannuation for someone like a working-holiday maker who's been here for a year, maybe only working 15 or 20 hours a week, adds the cost to the family, and it also adds complexity when they leave the country."

But ultimately, he said the law should be scrapped because it was contributing to a wider issue.

"It's pushing for giving them proper employment rights, so making sure people aren't having to get paid as a contractor or cash under the table and kind of more professionalising the whole industry," he said.

Both Ms Brown and Mr Hudson said the law was outdated, and many families using their platforms were already choosing to pay their nannies superannuation.

A spokesperson for federal Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino said in a statement the government was aware of the issue and "remained committed to ensuring the superannuation system is providing Australians with dignity and security in retirement".

"The government continues to monitor the operation of workplace and superannuation laws to ensure they remain fit for purpose and operate as intended for all workers," the statement said.

World.title: Australians with motor neurone disease fear losing fast-tracked NDIS
World.content:
Australians with motor neurone disease (MND) who have rapidly changing needs fear they will lose a priority pathway to access the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) under the federal government's planned changes.

The federal government has been warned the support system helping people with MND must move "faster than their disease" or the caring responsibilities will fall back unfairly onto their families.

Currently people diagnosed with MND are able to access the NDIS via a priority pathway overseen by staff who specialise in the disease that approves support packages within seven days.

But advocates and patients have been unable to get assurances that this option will remain under a planned overhaul of the NDIS announced last month.

More than 160,000 people to be kicked off NDIS as Labor overhauls eligibility Health Minister Mark Butler has unveiled the government's plan to curb the ballooning growth of the NDIS and save the budget a projected $35 billion over four years.

By 2027 the government wants access to the NDIS to be determined by a person's functional capability rather than diagnosis.

The average life expectancy is about 27 months for a person diagnosed with MND, a rapidly degenerative illness with no cure.

MND Australia chief executive Clare Sullivan said the priority pathway to the NDIS had been a "game changer" and "must be protected".

"This includes an assessment from someone with expertise in MND, quick decisions for funding, and a package allocation that meets their overwhelming needs," she said.

" MND is an excellent case study for how the NDIS is working … but there is huge community concern about the mooted changes. "

Todd Johnson, 50, was diagnosed with MND four years ago and said the disease needed a "different model and rapid responses" from the system that is looking after people.

"People living with MND are losing function every week and the system has to move faster than the disease," he said.

"If it moves slower, families have to carry the cost and then the patients suffer and dignity's lost."

Nidhi fought for 10 years to get on the NDIS. New cuts leave her 'in limbo' Nidhi Shekaran is one of thousands of NDIS participants waiting to learn if their services will be impacted as part of sweeping government reforms to the scheme.

Mr Johnson said the under the current NDIS priority pathway he was able to quickly access additional support as his disease progressed.

"When I first got diagnosed I was still working and I was fully healthy and walking around," he said.

"Now I'm in a wheelchair and I need a bit of support for things like getting dressed … and even getting to the point where just rolling over becomes difficult.

"But because the NDIS has been responsive it's been a wonderful experience because I don't wait too long for things."

Mr Johnson, who is the president of MND Victoria, said people in the community with the disease were "very nervous and quite frightened" about potentially losing both the priority pathway and aspects of their package funding.

"When you consider the pathway might not be there, it's really concerning because a package that's right today might be dangerously inadequate in three months," he said.

"If we go back into the [mainstream NDIS] system it won't keep up with our needs and the speed of the progressiveness of the illness."

Health Minister Mark Butler said the government would be "engaging deeply" with the disability community on the reforms it intends to pursue later in the year.

Mark Butler says participants with high needs will have access to critical supports. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"The thresholds and assessment process for determining substantially reduced functional capacity will be developed in the second half of 2026 based on expert advice from a technical advisory group," he said.

"Participants with the greatest level of needs will continue to have access to critical supports needed to live well and with dignity."

The changes flagged by Mr Butler in April are designed to slow the NDIS growth from a projected $70 billion to about $55 billion by 2030.

In addition to stricter eligibility, Labor plans to impose caps on some participant spending and tougher rules for providers to combat fraud and rorting.

World.title: Coalition's EV strategy risks appearing out of touch
World.content:
Various echo chambers have been chuntering for some time about a generous federal tax discount for electric vehicle buyers.

It is, we've been told, an outrageous example of "middle class welfare".

Yet it's a policy the government this week confirmed will be largely kept on the books in Tuesday's budget.

It's a tax break that applies to novated leases, which allow car buyers to pay the interest, registration, insurance, maintenance and operating costs of a vehicle from pre-tax income.

The effect of which is to lower a worker's taxable income and thereby reduce how much income tax they pay.

On a traditional novated car lease, the benefit is subject to fringe benefits tax (FBT), which erodes much of the advantage of paying for the vehicle from pre-tax income.

When Labor won the 2022 election it soon delivered on a promise to exempt FBT as a way to incentivise EV uptake at a time when most consumers were still on the fence about their benefits.

This week the government announced it would gradually phase-out the benefit.

From April, it will be limited to EVs costing no more than $75,000, down from the current ceiling of $91,000. Two years later, FBT will be reapplied minus a 25 per cent discount.

When Labor won the 2022 election it soon delivered on a promise to exempt the fringe benefits tax as a way to incentivise EV uptake. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

EV sales go up

One of the stated policy goals at the time it was introduced was to accelerate the flow of EVs into the second-hand car market.

That's because novated leases tend to last for between two to five years. Once they end, many of the vehicles are onsold.

The underlying logic was that while the FBT exemption would be taken up mostly by people on higher incomes, when they rolled those cars into the second-hand market it would be to the benefit of lower-income households.

Which is what now appears to be happening, just as demand for EVs accelerates because of the war in the Persian Gulf.

Second-hand EV sales leapt by 138 per cent between February and March to 7557, according to data from the Australian Automotive Dealer Association.

The biggest selling second-hand vehicles in April were Tesla Model 3s and Model Ys, which were the most popular cars when the FBT exemption first set off a wave of new buyers in 2023 and 2024.

The data supports the notion that those same cars are now hitting the second-hand market, as intended, where they're selling for between $25,000 and $40,000. Other models are cheaper still, particularly when factoring in the lower operating costs of EVs.

EV tax discount removed two days' worth of carbon emissions Two days' worth of carbon emissions were removed thanks to the $2 billion electric vehicle tax discount. But its supporters say that put 64,000 more EVs on the road, jump-starting the struggling industry.

Despite driving more cars into the second-hand market, the FBT exemption still triggers outrage from some commentators and politicians.

According to the Nationals leader Matt Canavan the policy is a "completely failed scheme", a statement that overlooks the fact buyers have adopted it with far greater vigour than was anticipated a few years ago.

The government regards that as a success.

Canavan again: "Providing an electric vehicle subsidy through the tax system has meant that the only people who benefit are those that are on the top tax bracket.

"And it shows the priorities of the modern Labor party, that they're forgetting the workers.

"This is not just middle class welfare, this is upper class welfare."

Canavan's criticism no doubt tickles rusted-on EV haters, but its logic rests on a misconception.

For one thing, there's an erroneous notion that the FBT exemption "costs" the budget a huge sum of money.

Treasury estimates the revenue foregone from the FBT exemption will be about $1.4 billion in 2025-26, a figure that will rise to $2.8 billion in 2028-29.

But removing the FBT exemption does not mean the budget would suddenly be flush with those dollars.

That's because the exemption is one of the primary reasons people take out a novated lease to buy an EV.

If it didn't exist, many would either opt to buy an EV outright, without a lease, or they wouldn't buy one at all.

In other words, tax collected from a reintroduced FBT would likely be less than the exemption is currently "worth".

Any politician promising to "bank" all of the purported lost tax in their budget accounting is fudging the books.

Treasury recognises this reality by categorising its confidence in the estimate of dollars foregone as "medium to low".

Loading

Climate wars won via incentives

People who choose EVs do so for two primary reasons, according to a Redbridge poll (of 2,269 people who have a novated lease) that was taken in March and April on behalf of the National Automotive Leasing and Salary Packaging Association.

Number one, among the top three reasons nominated for buying an EV — at 65 per cent of those surveyed — was "saving money".

Next — at 57 per cent — was "qualifying for the FBT discount".

There's then a gap to the next reason, with 39 per cent "reducing dependence on petrol and diesel".

"Doing something for the environment" or "lowering carbon emissions" was 20 per cent and 29 per cent respectively.

Cost and the FBT exemption are the main catalysts, a finding that suggest the "climate wars" are being won quietly on incentives and technology rather than reactionary zealotry.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

If the benefits that underlie decarbonisation are better for consumers — cheaper, more reliable and less vulnerable to the consequences of military overreach by a distant ally — they'll embrace it.

Furthermore, interest in EVs appears to have become decoupled from political leanings, the Redbridge polling suggests, with significant implications for right-leaning parties.

It shows, unsurprisingly, some 96 per cent of Greens voters say they are "very/somewhat likely" to make their next vehicle an EV, followed by 92 per cent of Labor voters.

More notable is that Coalition voters are close behind, with 87 per cent mulling an EV.

And most surprising of all? Nearly three in four (72 per cent) of One Nation voters are eager to buy one.

The war in the gulf has demonstrated how reliance on fossil fuels can hurt lower income households the most.

Often in commuter suburbs where public transport options are poor, those same families are now seeking an alternative.

Many are conservative voters. Which risks making the Coalition's ongoing attempt to kill the FBT exemption look out of touch.

Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

World.title: Keeping 'ISIS brides' out of sight will not make Australia safer
World.content:
Anthony Albanese has played a cynical political game over the so-called "ISIS brides".

For months, the prime minister talked tough on the four women and nine children who arrived in Australia on Thursday — and on the remaining families in Syria — while acknowledging he had no legal means to prevent their return.

His harsh words have not been matched by a sense of urgency about the resurgence of the Islamic State terrorist group in Australia, nor about the security gaps being exposed by the royal commission into the Bondi attack.

The political storm over the families has consumed the oxygen that should be directed at a far more pressing problem: Australia's homegrown terrorism crisis.

Keeping these families out was never a serious option and pursuing it as one has come at a cost.

The reality both sides of politics have refused to state plainly is that "out of sight, out of mind" is the most dangerous response to terrorism.

Known quantities like these families can be monitored. Australia's growing cohort of radicalised citizens at home are not as easily tracked.

The women and children left the Al Roj camp in Syria late in April, with plans to travel to Australia. (ABC News: Baderkhan Ahmad)

The women and their ties

To argue for their return while acknowledging the security risk they pose requires holding an uncomfortable truth.

The women who returned this week had close ties to significant ISIS figures.

Zahra Ahmed, 33 — the only of the four who is yet to be charged — is the widow of Australian ISIS recruiter Muhammad Zahab, who died in an airstrike in 2018.

A former Sydney maths teacher, Zahab recruited more than a dozen Australians to join Islamic State in Syria and rose to a leadership role within the terrorist group.

Zahab maintained ties to senior jihadists in Australia, including Wisam Haddad — the notorious pro-ISIS preacher whose Bankstown prayer centre was shut down after his connection to the Bondi Beach terrorists emerged.

Zahra Ahmed's father was suspected of funnelling money to ISIS through a fake charity, but claimed his family became trapped in Syria and he never supported terrorism.

Her mother, Kawsar Abbas, 53, and sister, Zeinab Ahmed, 31, were arrested at Melbourne Airport on arrival and charged with crimes against humanity — the first Australians to face such charges under domestic law — over the alleged enslavement of Yazidi women in Syria.

The fourth woman, Janai Safar, is the widow of an Australian ISIS operative and is now charged with membership of a terrorist group and entering a declared conflict zone.

She travelled to Syria with her cousin, who married an ISIS commander reported to be Tarak Khayat, who was sentenced to death in Iraq after organising a failed plot to bomb a flight from Australia.

Many of the "ISIS brides" claim to have been coerced or tricked into travelling to the so-called caliphate in Syria, before being incarcerated in the squalid Al Roj detention camp, after it crumbled in 2019.

Their ISIS connections carry real risks. What the political storm obscures is that Australian agencies are well-equipped to manage them — and the danger may be greater if these families remain abroad.

Loading

Why their return is the safer option

There is a firm consensus among security experts: it is safer to monitor these families within Australia than to leave them in Syria, beyond the reach of our legal and intelligence systems.

Australian citizens have a legal right to return home, regardless of what they may have done.

They will be watched by ASIO.

Courts can impose control orders, which can include home detention and communications restrictions, where there is evidence of imminent risk.

The government's decision to issue a temporary exclusion order to prevent just one of the women from returning from Al Roj to Australia suggests the intelligence on the others does not clear that threshold.

There is another strategic case for their return. Their years in Al Roj became a propaganda asset for Australia's ISIS network.

Wisam Haddad spent years highlighting their plight in lectures and online propaganda, portraying Australia as a nation that discriminates against Muslims.

That message lands because it contains some truth.

Failing to uphold citizens' rights while enforcing the law where evidence exists only sharpens it.

The new prosecutions will undoubtedly be seized on for the same propaganda purpose, but that is an argument for getting the legal process right, not for keeping the women stateless.

Returning extremists carry real risk, as history shows in Australia and abroad.

However, the risk of violence posed by these women is lower.

Under ISIS ideology, women were not combatants. They were wives, mothers, and in some cases recruiters and propagandists.

There are already more dangerous people operating freely within Australia.

Some men have been jailed for fighting with ISIS. Others remain free because of the challenges for authorities in gaining evidence overseas.

The returning children present a different challenge. They will need the best Australia can offer in deradicalisation intervention programs and welfare support. They did not choose to grow up in the caliphate.

Alongside monitoring, these are costly but necessary investments. The opposition puts the cost of monitoring high-risk individuals at $2 million per year, a figure the government has not contested.

The true crisis

The political energy spent on the "ISIS brides" has not been matched by serious attention to the deficiencies in Australia's counterterrorism architecture.

After being dragged into establishing the royal commission, the prime minister's response to its interim report last week was, in essence, nothing to see here.

Albanese accepted its modest recommendations but said "no urgent changes were required to keep Australians safe".

He deflected questions about a significant decline in the funding share allocated to counterterrorism by intelligence agencies.

The report showed the government had taken its eye off terrorism, despite ASIO's repeated warnings about a "probable" terrorist attack and the threat to Jews.

Investigating the return of the Islamic State terrorist group The Bondi Beach terrorist attack signalled the resurgence of the Islamic State terrorist group in Australia. For the past two years, ABC Investigations has tracked the group's revival, identifying key figures, mapping the network and raising questions about the response of police, intelligence agencies and governments.

For two years, an ABC investigation has documented the resurgence of ISIS in Australia and raised questions about the official response in the lead-up to Bondi.

Australia faces a crisis of radicalisation across the ideological spectrum. Some young people are falling through the gaps of deradicalisation and early intervention programs.

ASIO now assesses the terrorism threat at the same level as during the height of the caliphate.

There are at least 20 Australian women and children still hoping to return to Australia from Al Roj.

These families can be known quantities. They can be monitored by intelligence services and managed within a legal framework.

The real threat, as Bondi demonstrated, comes from those on the periphery, the people who slip through the cracks when the nation's attention is elsewhere.

In his response to the women and children who have been desperate to return to Australia, the prime minister has been fond of quoting his mother's advice: "If you make your bed, you lie in it."

It remains to be seen whether he will heed it himself.

World.title: Voters in Farrer set to elect new MP after three months in spotlight
World.content:
All eyes will be on the electorate of Farrer in southern NSW today as voters head to the ballot box in what could be a history-making by-election.

The former Coalition stronghold has been in the political spotlight ever since the resignation of local MP and deposed Liberal leader Sussan Ley more than three months ago.

"We've had more politicians here in Griffith than we've had in our entire history," former Griffith Business Chamber president Paul Pierotti said.

"We've been calling out the wrongdoings in these communities for a very long time, and now it seems [almost] every candidate is supporting the policies we've been trying to pursue.

" Where have they all been up until now? "

Paul Pierotti warns the incoming member for Farrer that voters will demand action on issues raised ahead of the by-election. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

The vast electorate covers nearly 16 per cent of the state, including the border city of Albury, the multicultural industrial hub of Griffith, and dozens of communities reliant on irrigated agriculture, such as Deniliquin, Leeton, Jerilderie and Narrandera.

Farrer has been a safe Coalition seat since its creation in 1949, but 12 candidates are now vying to become its next local member.

One Nation's David Farley and independent Michelle Milthorpe are considered the frontrunners, amid ongoing discontent with the major parties.

The electorate of Farrer covers 126,563 square kilometres, or nearly 16 per cent of New South Wales. (Supplied: Sussan Ley)

Carol Oataway is the mayor of Hay, which sits in the centre of the electorate.

She has welcomed the unprecedented levels of attention on the electorate, saying it has highlighted to the nation the important role the region plays in producing food, fibre and renewable energy.

But Cr Oataway said she was now eager for the campaigning to come to an end.

"I am looking forward to having a local member we can begin working with again," she said.

"We've been a while now without one, and there are times when you want to advocate and we don't have a member."

Carol Oataway says the lack of a local MP has been felt in Farrer. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

With no Labor candidate standing, whoever wins will have to work with the federal government to act on the pledges made during the campaign.

"I think they're going to have to work very hard to do that," Cr Oataway said.

" They've made these promises. As soon as they're elected they need to start getting to work with the government so we can see progress on some of these things. "

Mr Pierotti said the electorate would expect whoever won the seat to deliver action from Canberra.

"Anyone who ignores that, it will be at their peril," he said.

"These regional communities will no longer tolerate being treated with contempt and there will be significant backlash."

The Australian Electoral Commission said yesterday that nearly 50,000 voters, or 40 per cent of those enrolled in Farrer, had already cast their vote.

Polls open at 8am AEST.

World.title: Military parades and promises of peace ring hollower than ever
World.content:
Images of mass military parades across vast parade grounds in Moscow, Beijing and other homes of regimes on the "other side" of the Cold War were a regular part of nightly television viewing, for those of us of a certain age.

They have since become a trope in historic montages and pop culture clips.

Goosestepping disciplined troops and tank commanders saluting from their turrets, watched by groups of sullen, ageing men in fur hats and great coats dripping with medals.

Such parades don't entirely go away. China lifted the genre to a new standard last September to celebrate the 80th Anniversary of its WWII Victory over the Japanese and, of course, casually just underscore to the world how it has truly arrived as a home of high-tech military gear.

In Moscow this weekend, there will be something struggling not to be too embarrassingly revealing.

May 9 is Victory Day in Russia — the anniversary of the Soviet victory over Nazi Germany.

But it has had to be downgraded, partly because of security threats. Ukraine has actually hit sites in Moscow with drones near the Kremlin.

Vladimir Putin reportedly asked for a ceasefire to allow the march to proceed. There won't be any tanks or ballistic missiles on display.

Six months ago, the analysis around Russia's war with Ukraine was that, no matter the sense of the stalemate during the brutal winter, there was a relentless logic to Russia eventually winning through sheer weight of economic power based in its resources and political stubbornness.

That's not the case anymore, despite the gains that have come to the country's coffers from the surge in oil and gas prices.

Russian President Vladimir Putin ‌will be subjected to extra security in case of a Ukrainian attack when Russia celebrates Victory Day May 9. (Reuters: Sputnik/Mikhail Metzel)

A series of ineffective ceasefires

It's only nine months since Donald Trump left the world gasping by hosting Putin at a summit in Alaska, despite the warrant for the Russian leader's arrest on war crimes, and essentially being humiliated by a much cannier player who came for a couple of hours, owned a joint press conference, then went away again with nothing being achieved.

Those were the days when Trump liked to publicly associate himself with strongmen like Putin.

You don't hear quite so much of that these days.

Now the reporting is of a Russian leader who spends his life in bunkers, who hasn't been seen in public for two months, and who faces increasing speculation that he may be toppled.

Next week Trump goes to Beijing to meet President Xi Jinping, in a summit he had to postpone because the war the US started — along with Israel — against Iran wasn't going so well.

This week it emerged that Trump called off his Project Freedom plan to provide safe passage for vessels around the Strait of Hormuz because Saudi Arabia refused to let its bases and airspace be used to support it. (Reuters: Annabelle Gordon)

That war is going even worse now — although, technically, there is now a ceasefire in place — given there seem to be daily reminders that the US doesn't know how to get out of that war.

Of course there are actually three ceasefires in place: with Iran, with Hamas in Gaza, and between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

But these are the sorts of ceasefires you have when you don't have a ceasefire.

Over Thursday and Friday, the US and Iran shot directly at each other. The US hit sites in Iran. Iran fired on US vessels in the Persian Gulf. The two sides dispute who fired first. But it was an escalation in the tensions either way.

Notably, Iran said that the US had broken the ceasefire. The US, as it did earlier in the week, said Iran hadn't broken the ceasefire.

The framing of what happened was as revealing as the event itself: the US doesn't want the ceasefire to end.

Others would dearly like it to end.

Loading

In Israel, the media is full of alarm that the US may withdraw from this conflict without finishing the job. It has continued its own conflicts with Iranian proxies Hamas and Hezbollah even though ceasefires are also supposed to be in place in Gaza and Lebanon.

Having not been consulted about the latest mooted peace deal, it seemed a pointed rejection of any US sway of Israel's actions that it launched its first attack on Beirut in a month, just hours after the story was leaked. Israel is making clear it will be fighting, whatever the Americans do.

At least 846 people — including many women and children — have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire began, and thousands injured, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. Israel says that five of its soldiers have been killed in the same period.

Those who have been in Gaza in recent weeks say the sounds of Israeli drones overhead are a constant, frightening part of daily life. There are few signs that Hamas will give up its weapons.

In Lebanon, more than 120 people, including women and children, have been killed in the past week alone, according to Lebanon's health ministry.

Hezbollah has proved itself able to keep attacking Israel, despite Israel displacing a million people from the south of the country and destroying villages and civilian infrastructure.

Loading...

When words mean little

Even by the increasingly bizarre standards of the Trump administration, the warped sense of reality around world events is stretching.

Victory parades in a country at war in a five-year conflict, which has cost one million lives and needs a ceasefire to go ahead. Ceasefires where people still keep getting killed and where there is no confidence that the underlying causes of the conflict have been either settled or eliminated.

Yet we talk persistently of peace deals, despite the White House "announcing" via strategic leaks that one is just around the corner no fewer than five times in the past three weeks.

Information and propaganda wars are part of conflict. But the addiction to announcements in the world of media and social media — and the US president's addiction to feeding coverage about himself — has created the same sort of asymmetry with Iran in the war of words as many commentators observed were in place, in reverse, in terms of military power between the two combatants.

Increasingly it is the countries that find themselves in the physical middle of the bigger Iran-US conflict who are making a material difference to the way it is conducted.

Israel was always a major combatant. But its "side wars" in Gaza and Lebanon are playing a significant role in the bargaining over a larger peace deal since Iran insists Lebanon has to be part of the deal.

Loading...

The Gulf countries, too, are increasingly playing a role. This week it emerged that Trump called off his Project Freedom plan to provide safe passage for vessels around the Strait of Hormuz because Saudi Arabia refused to let its bases and airspace be used to support it.

Saudi, unlike some of its Gulf neighbours, is not so totally dependent on being able to ship out of the Strait of Hormuz but it is still affected by the crippling of world trade.

But it saw the plan as an escalation. It still tries to walk a line between the US and Iran. And it has links with Pakistan. But, pragmatically, it also knows that if things do escalate, the Iran-aligned Houthis can put the same block on the Red Sea as Iran has on the Strait of Hormuz — which really would hit the Saudis.

Closer US allies in the Gulf have also once again being paying the price of the stand-off with attacks on the UAE being seen by Iran as a slightly less provocative proxy for attacking the US directly.

Despite Trump's disdain for his allies, the significant damage to US bases and military assets in the Middle East that are increasingly being reported means his military's physical options now seem more constrained.

Before the revelation about the Saudi position on its airspace, flight trackers were noticing unusual levels of military aircraft activity out of Tel Aviv at the beginning of this week.

The US may have 50,000 troops and all sorts of overwhelming hardware on a parade of sorts in the Middle East.

But it's not much help if you can't land it anywhere. And the risks of using it have become part of the war of words about this conflict.

Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

World.title: Biofuels could ease our energy woes. But the industry says it needs a mandate
World.content:
Billions of dollars worth of investment will flow if the federal government mandates a percentage of biofuels be added to the nation's fuel supply, major investors say.

If the government makes a definitive decision on biofuels, superannuation investor Danny Elia told ABC News he could raise funds immediately to build a refinery, starting a process to lower fuel prices for Australian consumers.

"I would turn up to my investment committee tomorrow, asking for the support to invest in what would be our first plant, which would produce 8 per cent equivalent of the country's aviation fuel," the head of infrastructure assets at IFM Investors said.

"We would look to invest in the order of about $3 billion for the first plant, and we hope the second would be [built] shortly after that.'

Danny Elia helps look after $266 billion in investments on behalf of super funds and their members. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

Fuel security has been in the spotlight since the Middle East war sent shockwaves through global oil markets and raised questions about potential shortages in Australia.

Biofuels, made from organic matter, have been positioned as a renewable alternative to fossil fuels that could be made here, bolstering fuel supply.

On Wednesday, the prime minister announced more than $10 billion would be spent on bolstering Australia's fuel security, including expanding onshore reserves and exploring the feasibility of more local refining.

This week's announcement focused on getting and storing more crude-oil-based fuels, however last September, the government also announced $1.1 billion in grants to promote the expansion of biofuel production.

Farmers ready to supply biofuel raw materials

Australia currently imports 77 per cent of its refined fuel needs. The rest is refined here, but largely from crude oil imports.

In February, only nine barrels of every 100 used here were actually pumped out of the ground in Australia or its waters.

What would you like to see in the federal budget? We want to know what issues matter to you ahead of the federal budget. Have your say.

Agricultural groups have positioned themselves as the short and long-term solution to our fuel sovereignty problem, while building a biofuels industry that adds value to crops Australia already ships out.

"Farmers already supply products that power biofuel industries overseas," said National Farmers' Federation chief executive officer Mike Guerin.

" It's only logical and smart to support a domestic industry. "

Australia has the ingredients to make biofuels, but what has held them back is the lack of consistent demand that would allow big investments.

$3b super investment ready and waiting

IFM is the investment manager for Australia's enormous industry superannuation funds. It had $266.1 billion in funds under management at the end of last year, so Mr Elia is not kidding around.

The plant would be built next to Ampol's refinery in Lytton, a suburb of Brisbane, and be ready to go in five years.

Crop giant GrainCorp is involved as well, and is set to build a plant to crush canola for the new refinery.

Canola crops are a key component of biofuels. (ABC South East SA: Elsie Adamo)

It shows the potential scale of biofuels, but also demonstrates the reason Australia's biofuel industry is so small, despite having vast amounts of land, ingredients and potential.

Mr Elia said the market needed strong signals about demand to trigger the kind of long-term investment required.

More than $10 billion to boost fuel supplies and emergency stockpiles More than $10 billion will be spent bolstering Australia's fuel security, as the federal government attempts to shield the nation from the long-term consequences of the Iran war.

If it got them, Australia could produce a billion litres of low-carbon fuel by 2030 or 2032 and "grow exponentially from there", Mr Elia said.

"If we put all our energy and power into it, we could probably get close to 100 per cent of aviation [fuel] by about 2040, for example," he said.

"If you spread that across aviation and broader transport, like diesel, probably something in the order of about 30 per cent to 40 per cent of [liquid fuel] by 2040."

Not a supply problem, a lack of demand

Biofuels like sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and biodiesel are more expensive to produce in Australia than imported fossil fuels like crude oil.

Can Australia grow its own jet fuel? Australia exports billions of dollars worth of canola seed to make sustainable jet fuel that is sold back to us. This is what it will take to make it here.

With global prices for liquid fuels currently elevated by the conflict in the Middle East, they are competitive.

But that has not always been the case, and it is not expected to persist if the situation stabilises and global crude oil prices fall.

In this scenario, locally produced fuel would become more expensive than imported products, which currently satisfy close to 80 per cent of Australia's liquid fuel needs.

Without consistent decades-long demand, the Australian industry has said it cannot expand to reach sufficient size and breadth.

Mark Brown, the chair of the International Energy Agency's Bioenergy Technology Collaboration Programme, said if investors were going to be asked to spend billions on biofuels, they needed to know they would get a return.

Mark Brown is director of the Forest Research Institute at the University of the Sunshine Coast and a world expert in biofuels. (ABC News: Jake Kearnan)

"Any investor is looking for confidence. Certainty and confidence that when they put their money into the market, there's an opportunity to succeed," Professor Brown said.

A so-called "demand-side" mechanism, such as a government mandate that a certain percentage of fuel must be blended with biofuels, would build that confidence among investors.

Professor Brown pointed to overseas examples as evidence.

"Where we see bioenergy or renewable fuels having success, they have been supported or underpinned by things like fuel mandates that promote blending and create those market certainties that allow the investment to flow," he said.

Calls for legislated biofuel mandates

Barbara Kiss worked for General Motors for more than 24 years, most recently as the director of emissions compliance.

Now a consultant, she has worked with ethanol producer Manildra Group, an agribusiness that manufactures food and industrial products.

She spoke to the ABC about sugarcane biofuel, which is blended with petrol and used in standard cars and light vehicles.

A sugarcane refinery belonging to the Manildra Group. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"In the US, the demand-side mechanism ended up being a mandate," she said.

"The federal government just said, 'We're going to do this. We're going do this across the board. It's the right thing to do for all of these reasons.'"

Now E15 — a mix of petrol and up to 15 per cent ethanol — was available at more than 90 per cent of US fuel stops, Ms Kiss said.

Loading...

Ethanol is perhaps the easiest biofuel to increase the use of, as it's already in the Australian market and it does not require the modifications that fuels like biodiesel do.

Ms Kiss said an education campaign about the benefits of ethanol-blended petrol, and a legislated mandate to make it more available, were what Australia needed to boost consumption.

The body representing sugarcane growers shared similar sentiments.

"An enforced ethanol mandate would build demand and therefore justify new investment in supply, which would underpin new diversified revenue streams for our industry," Canegrowers chief executive officer Dan Galligan said.

What are the downsides to biofuels?

Aside from the higher cost, some people have raised concerns about the environmental impact on land used to farm feedstock, and competition for agricultural land between food and fuel suppliers.

Australia has a small biofuels industry, and most of the output is exported. More than 70 per cent of our canola is exported to other countries, which crush and convert it to biofuels.

"Look, it's still way behind the rest of the world," said Mr Elia, from IFM Investors.

" We currently, effectively, bankroll the rest of the world's decarbonisation and fuel security. "

World.title: Didn’t retire with ‘enough’? Here’s how to make the most of it
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementRetirement living Opinion Didn’t retire with ‘enough’? Here’s how to make the most of it Bec Wilson Money contributor May 9, 2026 — 5:16am

May 9, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I spent the latter half of this week at the Financial Counselling Australia conference, and it really brought something into focus for me. Many Australians aren’t retiring in comfort. We don’t talk nearly enough about what retirement looks like – or how to plan for it – if you don’t have a lot of money. We also don’t rave about financial counsellors enough and how they help people in tough situations, or who are deep in debt, to get back on track. Living a great life in retirement goes far beyond your bank balance. Louise Kennerley We tend to talk about retirement as if it’s something people move into by choice, confidently and with excitement. You’re expected to build up your super, pay off your home and step away from work with a fair bit of control over what comes next. But that’s not how it’s playing out for everyone right now. In fact, close to half of Australians retiring today rely on the age pension for a significant part of their income, and only a third or so retire by choice.



So what does retirement planning look like for people who don’t have “enough”, who didn’t get the chance to plan or who step away from work because their health shifts or caring responsibilities take over? In that world, it’s not about optimising your retirement and choosing the date. It’s about learning to live with choices that may have been forced upon you and making the best of the opportunities you do have. It’s not so much about how much super you have as a lump sum, but how much income that generates, and what you choose to draw down. Rebuilding your financial confidence is the first step, and the best way to do that is to understand how the financial systems that support retirement work, and how much money you can rely on coming in from passive income sources such as the age pension or superannuation. The age pension in Australia can be accessed from 67 years of age if you pass the assets and income test. It pays $31,223 a year for single people and $47,070 a year for couples at present, acting as the base layer of income that many people lean on in their later years.



Alongside this, they could add rent assistance, and the benefits from the pensioner concession card that every pensioner can access. If you’re caring for a loved one full-time and have not turned 67, you may be able to access the Carer Payment and concessions, a similar amount to the age pension. Then you look at how you can combine the age pension or other benefits with income from your super fund if you’re over 60. Editor's pick Opinion

Retirement living The silent deadline that could make or break your retirement Bec Wilson Money contributor The median super balance for people aged 60-64 in Australia is $219,773 for men and $163,218 for women. But it’s less about how much super you have as a lump sum than how much income that generates, and what you choose to draw down each year. That’s the important calculation – and the one that will build confidence in your situation. In retirement, the income from super on balances up to $2 million is tax-free once you move your super into a retirement phase account – an investment account that you must physically open with your super fund and deposit the funds into.



This is important to know because it is fundamentally different from how income works when you’re working. The wage you planned around when you were working was pre-tax, or gross, income so most people in the workforce lose 30-35 per cent or more of their income in tax before they start spending on the cost of living. In retirement, your income from the age pension sits below the tax-free threshold, and the income from a small super balance is tax-free. You can access your super from the age of 60, if you cease a role or are unemployed, or 65 if you’re working. If you’re still working between 60 and 65, you can access a transition-to-retirement strategy that allows you to draw out up to 10 per cent of your super each year, tax-free, as an income stream. This can be used in some clever ways: to supplement a part-time job that might not earn you enough to pay all your living costs, for instance; or, to contribute actively into super, leveraging the lower tax – 15 per cent – contribution rate on the first $30,000 of concessional contributions each year. All drawing out the income through the retirement system, tax-free. People with moderate balances should stop assuming they’re heading for a second-rate retirement just because they don’t have a seven-figure super balance. Getty Images Once your super is in the retirement phase, you have to draw down a percentage of the balance based on your age. It starts at 4 per cent of the balance up to the age of 65, then rises to 5 per cent from 65 to 74, then 6 per cent from 75 to 79, and so on.



That means a man with a median balance at age-pension age could be drawing close to $11,000, and a woman $8100, and then they’d combine this with the age pension to estimate their accessible income. A couple with median incomes might be able to add $18,100 at that conservative 5 per cent drawdown rate. In fact, there’s quite a bit of research to support a drawdown rate of 6 per cent or even 7 per cent in the early years of retirement, if the market is behaving well. Editor's pick Opinion

E-commerce How to spot the sinister tricks retailers use to manipulate your spending Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor On top of this, if you’re in good health and able, you might want to work a part-time or casual job to supplement these income streams. You can earn up to $7800 a year without seeing your age pension tapered. Once you’ve grasped the basics of the age pension and super, housing is the next big issue. And it is big. Rent assistance for someone in retirement today usually offers a subsidy of close to only $220 a fortnight – not even enough to make a dent on renting a room in a major capital city, let alone an entire flat or townhouse.



So finding housing that you can afford and that offers long-term stability is important. And to achieve this, many people leave our capitals for second- and third-tier cities where rents are a little lower, particularly when work is not the reason to stay. All these things are designed to help you secure a modest income that you can plan your life around. And that life is important. Once your income is secure, and you’ve established how you can live within your means on relatively passive income sources, the next job to do is work on your health – and focus on your happiness, fulfilment, sense of purpose and belonging: these are the real ways to have an epic retirement. First, your health is simple, and I want you to prioritise it. Focus on three things: good nutrition, regular exercise, and proactively preventing chronic disease. Get a breast scan, do the bowel cancer test, get regular dental checks, and watch your blood pressure. Then, work on your sense of purpose. When you worked, you traded time for money. Now you get to choose to do things that don’t pay in dollars but in happiness and purpose.



So I want you to take time to think about what you enjoy doing, and to explore the skills that you’ve enjoyed using at different times in your life. Write them down. Then think about the things you’re passionate about – maybe that’s helping people; perhaps it’s a love of plants or animals, or a cause you believe in. Then, consider what your values need from you to be aligned, and start exploring ways you could use your time, skills and passions in the years ahead for fulfilment. Life might have thrown you some curveballs, but you can still make your retirement epic. Bec Wilson is author of the bestseller How to Have an Epic Retirement and the newly released Prime Time: 27 Lessons for the New Midlife. She writes a weekly newsletter at epicretirement.net and hosts the Prime Time podcast. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: How to spot the sinister tricks retailers use to manipulate your spending
World.content:
MoneySavingE-commerce Opinion How to spot the sinister tricks retailers use to manipulate your spending Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor May 9, 2026 — 5:15am

May 9, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The only financial game in town right now is cutting your costs. But you will never do so effectively if you’re not across the “dark patterns” that subtly influence your spending. Forget straight-up digital marketing and targeting; dark patterns are sinister techniques online retailers use to manipulate consumers into parting with money they didn’t intend. Beneath the broad term lies a bunch of powerful psychological strategies designed to entice, coerce and even panic you into purchasing. Adding to cart can provide the rush of shopping, without costing a cent. Getty Indeed, they have become so pervasive online, even from reputable companies, that there is a current bill to amend Competition and Consumer Law to make it clear that businesses “must not manipulate consumers or unreasonably distort the environment in which consumers make or are likely to make decisions and in ways that are going to try and cause those consumers detriment”. Because while there are some protections in place under the law in terms of misleading and deceptive conduct, there is nothing to prevent more insidious techniques. You will no doubt recognise strategies such as this:



“Huge never-before-seen discounts” – bagging a bargain gives us a hit of a brain hormone called dopamine, which is seductive and also addictive.

“Only two left”, when there are likely thousands. This is usually layered on top of a discount to pressure you into making an immediate purchase rather than giving you the chance to wait and think better of it.

The countdown at the top of the screen, maybe saying you only have 30 seconds left to buy the product, or it/the discount disappears forever – again, engineering panic purchasing.

Gamified shopping, which you see particularly with overseas mass-market retailers. You “spin this” or “roll that” to qualify for a percentage off your whole shopping cart or sometimes even specific free items. If you stick with it, you will find there are extreme qualifying conditions, but you’ve already been shown and possibly taken a shine to said items – and might buy more. Editor's pick Opinion

Budgeting The top five money mistakes you’re probably making right now Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor Often, dark patterns constitute false advertising, but that’s difficult to prove. Having said that, the Federal Court has recently fined online mattress and bedding company Emma Sleep $15 million for exactly this. The penalty is for false or misleading online sale representations over the course of three years, between 2020 and 2023. But the form this took was enormous discounts that, when you clicked through to buy, were subject to a countdown of the sale’s imminent end. But in fact, out of 74 products, 58 had never been above the discounted price. The “original” price had never been charged.



The good thing is that if you are aware of all the pervasive applications of dark patterns, it is easier to resist them. But better still – in the name of saving money – is to avoid being subjected to them. Here are some recent steps I’ve taken to reduce my online targeting. Unsubscribe en masse. My email inbox had become absolutely jammed with marketing spam – you know, from basically everything I’ve ever bought – so I devoted some time to hitting the “unsubscribe” link on everything. Sometimes it’s a multi-step process, but it’s worth it. The option to instantly use a card that is saved on your phone, say with Apple Pay, lubricates spending that little bit too much. Use a browser that won’t track you. For the same reason as above – your probably rich online purchasing history – what you are served up online (or on social media) is a rich tapestry of your personal penchants. You’ve been comprehensively mapped and tracked for a long time now. And deals and discount on things you actually want are incredibly difficult to resist. Use Google? If you haven’t turned off permissions, it is analysing your every search to serve you with “personalised ads”.



A browser called Brave has no ads. What’s more, a search engine called DuckDuckGo is its default and won’t remember your searches either. Demote social media ads. If you are clicking on any link presented to you not only via email or message right now, but in a sponsored social media post, then you’re living dangerously. There has been a dramatic rise – prompting an ACCC warning – about online ghost stores, ones that don’t really exist. Typically, ads for such stores will use all the emotional tricks in the conversion book, including creating a sense of urgency that a much-loved actual-and-known brand may be sadly closing down … and, again, you have a very limited time to snare an extreme bargain. You can also, to an extent, control what you are served up. It depends on the platform, but each has a mechanism to either block or minimise ads for particular products or product types. For example, three dots appear at the right-hand side of ads on Facebook, that let you “hide” or “see less” of such ads in future.



Avoid “click to pay”. The option to instantly use a card that is saved on your phone, say with Apple Pay, lubricates spending that little bit too much. Editor's pick Opinion

Federal budget The great Australian dream is dying. Unless Labor acts now, it’s gone forever Max Yong Money contributor There is no cause for spending “pause”, which completely (what behavioural finance experts call) “decouples” the purchase from payment pain. And that’s even more so than just physically reaching for a credit card. A better approach – always – is to put what you think you want in your shopping cart and then just delay, as policy. Wait a day, go back to the store and purchase what you now deem sensible to buy. Or don’t. Because our shopping desires on a platter along with dark patterns make for heady spending temptation.



Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is the author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram.
